interest: This file offers an illuminating look at the bureaucratic and legal struggle between civilian agencies (State and Commerce) and military authorities (SCAP and the War/Army Department) over the commercial and scientific exploitation of Japanese technical know-how. It highlights how U.S. officials sought to replicate the lucrative technical intelligence gathering conducted in post-war Germany, only to be constrained by General MacArthur's insistence on absolute occupation control and reluctance to accommodate Allied missions. Additionally, the documents reveal how multilateral obligations in the Far Eastern Commission, domestic patent legislation (H.R. 4070 and Executive Order 9604), and emerging Cold War security anxieties complicated efforts to open Japanese industrial and patent secrets to Allied nations.
overview: This file documents interdepartmental policy discussions and negotiations within the United States Government—primarily involving the Department of State, the War Department (Civil Affairs Division), the Department of Commerce (Office of Technical Services and Publication Board), and SCAP—between August 1947 and February 1948 regarding proposals to dispatch Allied scientific and technical investigators to occupied Japan. Following British requests and proposals by John C. Green to investigate and exploit Japanese scientific and industrial advances similarly to operations in post-war Germany, U.S. policymakers confronted SCAP's objections to large missions, jurisdictional and property issues concerning Japanese patents and Zaibatsu assets under JCS 1380/15 and SWNCC 369, and U.S. legal policies under H.R. 4070 and Executive Order 9604. The records detail efforts to draft a compromise policy for a restricted multilateral team under SCAP's supervision, coordinate through the Far Eastern Commission (FEC) and the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC/SANACC), and resolve Army Department resistance regarding national security, culminating in consideration of an Australian proposal in the FEC.

subfiles.about: J. C. Green provides feedback on the draft SWNCC paper concerning the investigation of Japanese technology, endorsing SCAP control and urging coordination to avoid redundant data collection.
subfiles.summary: J. C. Green replies to Raymond Vernon's memoranda of September 23 and October 3 regarding the proposed SWNCC policy on investigating Japanese technology. Green strongly endorses proposed modifications placing the program under SCAP's direct control while restricting the Publication Board's role to U.S. technical information. He emphasizes the need to establish a clear channel with SCAP in Japan to verify what data already exists in occupation files prior to nominating and dispatching scientific investigators.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from J. C. Green to Raymond Vernon on SWNCC Paper for Investigation of Japanese Technology

subfiles.about: Roswell H. Whitman recommends revisions to the Japanese technology investigation plan to avoid Far Eastern Commission opposition by ensuring multinational participation under SCAP control.
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman of the Division of Economic and Social Affairs (OE) comments on the proposed plan for investigating Japanese technology, cautioning that excessive U.S. supervision and control over member selection and dissemination would trigger opposition in the Far Eastern Commission (FEC). He submits a redraft of paragraph 4 limiting the group to a maximum of 25 technical and scientific investigators from interested FEC countries under SCAP's authority. Under the revised plan, SCAP would screen and publish technical findings, withholding only military secrets, while John C. Green of the Publication Board would coordinate U.S. recruitment in consultation with other FEC nations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Roswell H. Whitman to Raymond Vernon on Program for Investigation of Japanese Technology

subfiles.about: J. C. Green explains that government funding for Japanese scientific exploration was dropped due to SCAP opposition in favor of an industry-supported volunteer effort.
subfiles.summary: In reply to an inquiry from Alfred W. Wells, John C. Green explains why an initial $200,000 budget estimate for government-sponsored scientific exploration in Japan—comparable to work carried out in post-war Germany—was eliminated from current and future fiscal requests. Green notes that SCAP strongly objected to large-scale operations in Japan, insisting instead that only a very small number of investigators be allowed under strict SCAP supervision. Consequently, Green decided that this modest activity could be easily handled through voluntary industry cooperation using his existing Washington recruiting staff without expending government funds.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from J. C. Green to Alfred W. Wells on OTS Funds for Japanese Exploitation

subfiles.about: Robert A. Fearey reports on War Department objections to proposed technical missions to Japan and recommends drafting a new SWNCC policy paper.
subfiles.summary: Robert A. Fearey advises John M. Allison that efforts to dispatch Allied technical missions to Japan have reached a stone wall due to War Department objections. Following discussions with CAD patent specialist Stevenson and a letter from General Eberle, Fearey reports the military's view that paragraph 24 of JCS 1380/15 and SWNCC 369 require a formal SWNCC decision and Joint Chiefs of Staff directive before SCAP can authorize inspection of Zaibatsu assets or patents. Fearey recommends that OE draft a new policy paper in consultation with IR, informally update British representatives, and prepare responses for upcoming department actions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Robert A. Fearey to John M. Allison on Technical Investigations in Japan

subfiles.about: Excerpts from post-surrender directives concerning the economic purge, the protection of Zaibatsu assets, and the publication of Japanese patents.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure sets forth key provisions from post-surrender occupation directives governing economic policy and industrial property in Japan. Paragraphs 23 and 24 of JCS 1380/15 mandate the removal of militant nationalists from influential economic positions and require the protection and maintenance of plants, equipment, patents, and records belonging to large Japanese industrial, financial, and research organizations. Paragraph 13 of Appendix C of SWNCC 369 directs the Japanese Patent Office to resume publication of patent gazettes and specifications to expedite disclosure of pending and unpublished patents, authorizing SCAP to assist in disseminating worthwhile technological data among Far Eastern Commission member nations.
subfiles.title: Enclosure: Extracts from JCS 1380/15 and SWNCC 369 on Japanese Economic Purge and Patents

subfiles.about: Brigadier General G. L. Eberle returns a draft cable to SCAP, stating that technical investigation proposals must be formally submitted to SWNCC and the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
subfiles.summary: Brigadier General G. L. Eberle, Acting Chief of the War Department's Civil Affairs Division, responds to Charles E. Saltzman regarding a draft cable to SCAP forwarded by the State Department on August 7, 1947. Eberle returns the cable without concurrence, explaining that the proposed dispatch of technical missions falls within the purview of paragraph 24 of JCS 1380/15 regarding the preservation of Zaibatsu property and relates to paragraph 13 of Appendix C of SWNCC 369. He advises that the proposed action must be formally considered and decided by both the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC) and the Joint Chiefs of Staff before directives are issued to SCAP.
subfiles.title: Letter from Brigadier General G. L. Eberle to Charles E. Saltzman on Draft Cable to SCAP

subfiles.about: Proposed cable to SCAP detailing a compromise plan for small British and American scientific missions and access to Japanese Patent Office data.
subfiles.from: Civil Affairs Division, War Department Special Staff
subfiles.summary: This draft cable communicates to SCAP a compromise proposal to permit two British and two American scientists into Japan to investigate scientific and technical advances, following up on earlier British requests and John C. Green's initiative. To address SCAP's prior objections regarding unilateral action and excessive numbers of Allied personnel, the plan invites other Far Eastern Commission governments to participate by surveying designated industries and grants FEC representatives access to the Japanese Patent Office. The cable emphasizes that under H.R. 4070 and Executive Order 9604, pre-1946 Japanese inventions and know-how are effectively placed in the public domain, allowing free and prompt public dissemination by the Publication Board without property compensation.
subfiles.title: Draft Cable from War Department Special Staff to SCAP on Technical and Scientific Investigations
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

subfiles.about: Robert A. Fearey explains the background of the stalled proposal for technical missions to Japan and justifies resubmitting the plan to SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Robert A. Fearey reviews the background of John C. Green's initiative to send an American technical mission to Japan, which had been rejected by SCAP in cable C-51591 in April 1947. Fearey explains that while further action had been deferred pending SWNCC and FEC consideration of a Japanese patent policy paper, renewed British requests and legal analysis by International Resources (IR) warrant approaching SCAP again. He argues that the proposed draft wire establishes a reciprocal, small-scale quota acceptable to both the British and Green, which should successfully resolve SCAP's practical and jurisdictional objections.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Robert A. Fearey to Japan-Korea Secretariat on Draft Wire to SCAP

subfiles.about: A draft paragraph explaining that H.R. 4070 and Executive Order 9604 eliminate legal barriers regarding Japanese patent rights and technical know-how.
subfiles.summary: This draft paragraph, prepared by J. Philips Furman of International Resources and cleared by telephone with Robert A. Fearey, clarifies the legal status of wartime Japanese patents and technical information. It explains that Section 3 of pending bill H.R. 4070 bars German and Japanese nationals from obtaining U.S. patents for inventions made prior to January 1, 1946, throwing such inventions into the public domain. It further notes that under Executive Order 9604, U.S. policy mandates prompt, free, and public dissemination of enemy scientific and industrial know-how without compensation, as has already been successfully implemented in occupied Germany.
subfiles.title: Draft Paragraph for Cable to SCAP on Japanese Patent Rights and Technical Know-How

subfiles.about: State Department draft cable proposing that SCAP allow two British and two American scientists to investigate Japanese technology, with findings published by the Publication Board.
subfiles.from: Robert A. Fearey and J. Philips Furman
subfiles.summary: This earlier version of the draft cable to SCAP, coordinated between the Office of Northeast Asian Affairs and the Division of International Resources, proposes allowing two British and two American scientists into Japan to inspect technical and scientific advances. It addresses SCAP's previous concerns regarding unilateral action by offering equal opportunities to other Far Eastern Commission countries to investigate individual industrial sectors. Citing H.R. 4070 and Executive Order 9604, the message asserts that Japanese pre-1946 patents and unpatentable know-how are considered public domain, authorizing John C. Green of the Publication Board to publish and disseminate all collected technical data.
subfiles.title: Draft Telegram to SCAP on British and American Technical Investigations in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

subfiles.about: Noel Hemmendinger refers General Eberle's non-concurrence letter to Robert A. Fearey to determine State's next procedural steps.
subfiles.summary: Noel Hemmendinger transmits Brigadier General G. L. Eberle's letter of August 21, 1947, to Robert A. Fearey in the Office of Northeast Asian Affairs following an earlier conversation. Hemmendinger requests Fearey's recommendation on what procedural action the State Department should take next in light of the War Department's refusal to approve the draft cable to SCAP.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Noel Hemmendinger to Robert A. Fearey on War Department Letter

subfiles.about: Text amendment instructing the addition of a sentence making Japanese Patent Office records available to Far Eastern Commission representatives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This drafting instruction slip from the Office of the Assistant Secretary directs that an additional sentence be inserted into the second paragraph of the proposed cable to SCAP. The sentence specifies that information in the Japanese Patent Office should also be made available to representatives of Far Eastern Commission member nations currently stationed in Japan. This revision was incorporated into the version of the cable reviewed by the War Department.
subfiles.title: Drafting Instruction for Cable to SCAP regarding Japanese Patent Office Information

subfiles.about: Alfred W. Wells reports on Army Department obstruction regarding Japanese technology and recommends adopting an Australian proposal pending in the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: Alfred W. Wells reports to Raymond Vernon on delays affecting SANACC policy papers regarding the investigation of Japanese technology. Wells reveals that Under Secretary of the Army William H. Draper Jr. refused to send a clarifying cable to SCAP regarding the Army's contradictory security arguments, leaving U.S. FEC representative General Frank R. McCoy without instructions on how to vote. With an imminent vote on an Australian proposal that closely mirrors the State Department's objectives, Wells recommends adopting the Australian paper as the basic policy and utilizing State's detailed draft to guide its implementation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Alfred W. Wells to Raymond Vernon on FEC Discussions and Australian Proposal
